section_title: Why does God give Moses the commands on stone?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 18 When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God.

context_lines: The mountain instructions end with something Moses can carry back to Israel: two stone tablets inscribed by God. God has already spoken His commands to the people; now Moses receives their written testimony. Deuteronomy identifies the writing as the Ten Commandments and connects the tablets with the words Israel heard at the mountain ([Deuteronomy 4:9–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/4.htm); [9:9–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/9.htm)).

The chapter closes with God giving His testimony. The next chapter turns to what the people have been doing while Moses is away. That contrast matters: the covenant is not simply an agreement Israel has devised, and the people’s response will be measured against what God has said.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) and [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/31.htm) understand God’s finger here as His direct power and authorship: the inscription comes from God. Both also explain the tablets as a lasting witness to His will; the verse does not describe the physical shape of God or state how the commands were divided between the two stones.
god_plan_lines: Paul later draws an explicit contrast between stone tablets and human hearts. The Corinthians are a letter from Christ, written by the Spirit of the living God on hearts rather than stone ([2 Corinthians 3:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_corinthians/3.htm)). He does not dismiss Sinai as something worthless: he calls its ministry glorious, then explains the greater glory of the Spirit’s life-giving work ([2 Corinthians 3:7–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_corinthians/3.htm)).

The connection shows a larger purpose than preserving instructions in writing. Through Christ, God is at work in the people who receive His word, giving life and making them a living testimony that others can read. The stone tablets belong to the unfolding story of that greater work.
